prize_parts.citation: for showing, with transparent and replicable research designs, how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, job polarisation and the adjustment of local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B009 with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. The reasoning is partly revised, and the chair's question is why. The work offers a clear conceptual idea (tasks and polarisation) together with designs that outside researchers can re-run. Those designs are import-competition exposure and local labour-market outcomes built from public census and administrative data. The finding of large, persistent local adjustment costs has survived many re-analyses and has changed the policy debate on trade and automation. Autor and Dorn (2013) is a task-based polarisation paper, so Dorn spans both the technology and the trade strand of the citation. I no longer rely on the argument I made in round 1 that Katz's education-and-technology work is too close to Goldin's recognised research. Fredriksson, Krusell and Enflo are right that the 2023 citation concerned women's labour-market outcomes, so the overlap is thematic. My reasons for Dorn over Katz are now narrower. First, a citation on labour demand, polarisation and local adjustment is credited exactly to these three. Second, the Katz strand is a long wage-structure tradition with several contributors, and Katz also appears in B050. The Katz trio is a defensible variant, and the choice is close. If the committee defines the achievement as the broad wage-structure and skill-premium account, I would prefer Autor, Hanson and Katz over my own set. My preference follows how the achievement is defined, not how many members hold which trio.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the shift-share exposure designs are the subject of live inference debate. The persistence and external validity of the China-shock estimates are still being refined, and a citation should not claim more than the replicated findings support. Excluding Katz is a real attribution cost. His skill-supply and skill-premium evidence is the longest-confirmed part of this literature, and it is more settled than the trade-shock magnitudes. Taking the narrower trade-shock-plus-polarisation framing means giving up some of that settled evidence. The three-name cap also leaves out Levy and Murnane on the task framework. The prize could be read as two discoveries (technology and trade) bundled into one. Finally, I cannot rule out that the round-1 split between the two trios means neither can reach six votes, and I do not treat that as evidence about merit.

responses.point: Teorell prefers Autor, Hanson and Dorn on the China-shock evidence, treats Katz's wage-structure work as a parallel contribution with a contestable boundary, and would accept the Katz version only if the committee decides the broader framing is the discovery.
responses.response: We reach the same trio for similar reasons, and I agree with how you structure the choice. The chair asked whether I would prefer the Katz trio under a broader definition. Yes, conditionally. If the committee decides the discovery is the whole technology, tasks, trade and wage-structure account, Katz fits it better than Dorn, and I would support Autor, Hanson and Katz. We differ slightly on the narrow version. I would not limit it to import competition, because Autor and Dorn (2013) on polarisation is part of why Dorn belongs, so my citation names labour demand and polarisation as well as local adjustment. I also withdraw my round-1 Goldin argument against Katz, since you and others showed the 2023 overlap is thematic.

responses.point: Krusell prefers Autor, Katz and Hanson. He argues that a citation spanning technology, trade and inequality needs Katz as the anchor of the long-run skill supply-and-demand evidence, and that dropping him leaves the less settled China-shock part.
responses.response: This is the strongest argument against my trio, and it changes how I weigh the maturity question. The skill-premium evidence is older and better confirmed than the trade-shock magnitudes, and my replication-based criterion favours it. I still hold my set for two reasons. The citation I propose is about labour demand, polarisation and local adjustment. It is not a full account of the skill premium, so Katz's anchor role is less necessary. And the shift-share debate is mostly about magnitudes and inference. The core finding of persistent local costs has survived re-analysis, so I do not think it is the weak link. If the committee adopts your broader definition, I would not oppose your trio. I would ask the committee to state openly that Dorn's omission follows from the cap.

responses.point: Hassler, the chair, prefers Autor, Hanson and Katz but calls Dorn in place of Katz a defensible variant if the committee prefers the trade-shock framing. He would word the citation around empirical labour-demand evidence, not the theory of automation, and he moved from B040 to B009 on identification grounds.
responses.response: Your wording constraint is one I share. I tested it on my own citation, which says how technological change and import competition reshape labour demand, polarisation and local labour markets. It rests on empirical designs and does not claim the task model or directed-technology theory, which would belong to Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu and Restrepo. I agree that B040 deserves less weight than I first thought after your move. The cross-country constitutional evidence is more specification-sensitive than the B009 designs. Your concession that the Dorn variant is defensible narrows the actual disagreement to one name, and I would put it to the committee as one definitional question. It would be wrong to resolve it by counting preferences.

responses.point: Boppart prefers B014 with Melitz and Helpman. He argues that the welfare-gain critique qualifies the citation rather than defeating it, and that wording around selection and reallocation, not large aggregate gains, handles the priority issue with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum.
responses.response: This partly answers my round-1 question, and it moves me on the welfare point. If the citation rests on selection and reallocation and not on the size of the gains from trade, the Arkolakis et al. critique matters less to me. It does not resolve the priority issue for me. Careful wording changes what the prize claims, but it does not change who established the exporter-premium facts and the quantitative-trade line that the framework builds on. You say Melitz's tractable selection model is distinct from that line, and I find that a reasonable argument, though I cannot settle it from this record. This is why I move B014 up to a named alternative, but I do not make it my preferred part.

responses.point: Friberg prefers B014. He argues that Krugman's 2008 prize concerned scale economies and representative-firm trade patterns, whereas Melitz put productivity-sorted selection at the centre, and that this produced testable predictions later confirmed in firm-level data.
responses.response: That answer changes my view on Krugman. I had counted the 2008 prize as covering part of this ground, and your distinction between representative-firm new trade theory and heterogeneous-firm selection is persuasive. The point about testable predictions confirmed in micro data is also the kind of evidence I value. After your response, the Krugman overlap is no longer a reason against B014 for me. The remaining reservations are priority claims and the size of welfare gains, and the second is now much reduced. This is the main reason B014 replaces B016 among my alternatives, together with my continued doubts about the mixed confirmation of taxable-income elasticities. I still rank B009 above it, because its debates concern magnitudes while the B014 priority question concerns who is credited.

responses.point: Andersson prefers B045 with Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. He argues that a methods contribution should be judged by whether it changed what can be measured and decided, and that BLP has thirty years of scrutiny, use in merger review and a relatively clean attribution. The chair asked whether alternative-listers see a path to preferring it.
responses.response: I accept your test, and it is why B045 remains one of my two alternatives. I do not discount a methods prize relative to a discovery prize, and BLP has been re-implemented across many datasets. The chair's question was whether I would see a configuration where it becomes preferred. I would if the committee judged B009 unsettled on both attribution and the technology-and-trade bundling. The BLP trio has a cleaner boundary than either B009 trio, and your answer on Bresnahan is clear. I would still want the citation limited to demand estimation and competition, so the research-programme prize you warn about does not appear. What keeps it below B009 for me is breadth of changed understanding and the visibility of the evidence. It is not a doubt about quality or maturity.

uncertainties: Whether the committee defines the B009 achievement as the broad technology, tasks, trade and wage-structure account (favouring Katz) or as polarisation and the trade-shock evidence (favouring Dorn). I can state a conditional preference for either trio, but I cannot tell which definition is more defensible from this record.
How persistent and externally valid the China-shock estimates are, and how far the shift-share inference debate should limit the wording of the citation.

Whether my citation separates the empirical contribution from the task theory (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo) cleanly enough, and whether the 2023 and 2024 prizes make the marginal contribution smaller. I now treat the overlap as thematic, but I rely on colleagues' descriptions of those prizes.
Whether B014's priority claims (Bernard, Jensen, Eaton, Kortum, Hopenhayn) are weaker than the Dorn-or-Katz choice or the bundling question in B009. I cannot resolve this from the supplied evidence.

Whether the split between the two B009 trios will prevent either from reaching a majority, in which case the committee may have to weigh B014's more uniform attribution against B009's broader evidence.
statement.conflict_note: No connection is apparent from my supplied profile to Autor, Dorn, Hanson or Katz (B009), or to the credited names in my alternatives B014 and B045. My frequent co-authors (Johannesson, Camerer, Pfeiffer, Holzmeister, Huber, Nosek, Rand, Fudenberg, Nowak) work in behavioural economics and metascience, and none is credited on a shortlisted entry. My SSE affiliation is shared with committee colleagues Andersson, Friberg and Strömberg, which Andersson also noted. I have no documented tie from this to any candidate. I disclose this without adjudicating and claim no independent verification.
